status_summary: As of 2026-10-08 no reassignment of election-related 18 U.S.C. 241 cases between DOJ divisions was found in either direction. The Justice Manual section the Mandate cites (JM 8-3.000, last modified 2022-12-19 as retrieved) still lists section 241 among the criminal civil rights statutes the Civil Rights Division oversees; the regulations (28 CFR 0.50, last amended 2019-01-25, and 0.55) already assign election-related 241 matters not involving race or color to the Criminal Division; later amendments to part 0 (the Tax Division transfer of 2025-12-10 and the National Fraud Enforcement Division rule effective 2026-08-24) do not touch election work; and the Election Crimes Branch page (updated 2026-10-06) still places the branch in the Criminal Division's Public Integrity Section. The Civil Rights Division has been active on election matters, mostly on the civil side: AP reported on 2025-05-03 an internal memo directing its Voting Section toward election-fraud and citizenship priorities (AP noted the section is a civil unit that does not investigate crimes), and on 2026-07-07 the division's head sent letters to the chief election officials of every state saying officers who knowingly keep noncitizens on voter lists or help them vote could face criminal liability; California Globe (2026-07-08) reports that the letter's closing paragraph says an intentional act to dilute citizens' votes could violate 18 U.S.C. 241, and the article, not the letter, says criminal prosecution runs through the Criminal Division or U.S. attorneys rather than the Voting Section; Votebeat's account does not name that statute, and neither source says which office would bring a 241 case. Other reports describe election-crime work as centered on the 93 U.S. attorney's offices: NOTUS reported on 2026-06-08 that the Election Crimes Branch has no permanent director and the Justice Manual requirement to consult the Public Integrity Section on election matters was suspended in June 2025, and Bloomberg Law reported on 2026-09-08 that the Deputy Attorney General's office told U.S. attorneys to prioritize noncitizen-voting cases. No 18 U.S.C. 241 election indictment by either division, and no order moving or confirming the allocation, was found; Executive Order 14248 (2025-03-25) sets election-law enforcement priorities but does not reassign any division's responsibilities.

timeline.event: Context: the Justice Manual section the Mandate cites for the current allocation (JM 8-3.000, Enforcement of Civil Rights Criminal Statutes) lists 18 U.S.C. 241 among the statutes overseen by the Civil Rights Division and its Criminal Section, with U.S. attorney's offices jointly responsible; the page was last modified on this date and does not address election matters.

Executive Order 14248 signed (Federal Register 2025-03-28): directs the Attorney General to prioritize enforcement against noncitizen voting, pursue information-sharing agreements with state election officials, and act on state voter-list maintenance; it does not reassign any division's responsibilities.

AP reports an internal Civil Rights Division memo (date not given) stating that the Voting Section will focus on election integrity, fraud, enforcing the March 2025 elections order and ensuring only citizens vote; AP notes that the department investigates and prosecutes voter fraud in a separate criminal-side division and that the Voting Section is a civil unit that does not investigate crimes. The report does not mention 18 U.S.C. 241.

NOTUS (as republished by The Washington Sun) reports the Election Crimes Branch has had no permanent director since its longtime head left, that most Public Integrity Section lawyers have departed, that DOJ appointed district election officers in each district, and that election-crime training sessions planned for 2026 did not take place. The report does not mention any reassignment of 241 cases between divisions.

The Civil Rights Division's Assistant Attorney General signs letters to the top election officials of every state and the District of Columbia saying officers who knowingly keep noncitizens on statewide voter lists or help them cast ballots could face criminal liability, and asking for compliance plans; California Globe reports the letter says an intentional act aimed at diluting citizens' votes could violate 18 U.S.C. 241, while Votebeat's account does not name that statute or say which DOJ office would prosecute, and a DOJ spokesperson described the aim as voluntary compliance.

The eCFR text of 28 CFR 0.50 (Civil Rights Division), current as of this date, lists the Criminal Division as handling 18 U.S.C. 241, 242, and 594 for voting and election matters not involving race or color discrimination or intimidation; 28 CFR 0.55 (current as of 2026-08-03) says the same. The eCFR version history shows section 0.50 was last amended on 2019-01-25, and a final rule creating the National Fraud Enforcement Division (published 2026-08-18, effective 2026-08-24) amends part 0 without mentioning election crimes.

Bloomberg Law reports that the Deputy Attorney General's office instructed all U.S. attorneys to prioritize election-integrity cases focused on noncitizen voting, urging charges under 18 U.S.C. 611 and false-registration statutes, and that a DOJ-hosted webinar on 2026-09-02 covered such cases; the report does not mention the Criminal Division, the Civil Rights Division or section 241.

DOJ's Election Crimes Branch page, last updated this date, still describes the branch as part of the Criminal Division's Public Integrity Section and says voting matters based on race, color, religion or national origin are handled by the Civil Rights Division; it does not mention 18 U.S.C. 241.

title: Move election-related 18 U.S.C. 241 prosecutions from Civil Rights to Criminal Division
uncertainties: Stage decision (not_started kept; diverged considered). Basis: the recommendation concerns where election-related 241 prosecutions are assigned. Searches in this pass (241 election indictments in 2025 and 2026; Civil Rights Division and Public Integrity Section election roles; the July 2026 Civil Rights Division letters; the Voting Section refocus) found no order, regulation or Justice Manual change in either direction and no 241 election indictment by either division. The Civil Rights Division's election activity found is civil (the Voting Section, which AP says does not investigate crimes) or takes the form of warning letters that a California Globe report says cite 241; letters are not charges and do not change who prosecutes. Election-crime enforcement reported elsewhere runs through the 93 U.S. attorney's offices, which the Justice Manual already shares with the Civil Rights Division for 241. diverged would apply if a DOJ order or an indictment showed the Civil Rights Division taking over or keeping election 241 prosecutions against the Mandate's recommendation; none was found, so a reader could reasonably choose diverged on the strength of the July 2026 letters and the reduced Public Integrity Section. Evidence limits: the 241 citation in the July 2026 letter rests on one outlet (California Globe, which names the statute) and a student newspaper (The Dartmouth, read but not cited) that names a 'Conspiracy Against Rights' provision; Votebeat's account does not name it (nor did a Reuters-credited report on the Fulton Sun site, read but not cited), and the letter itself was not retrieved. The NOTUS facts (director vacancy, suspended consultation requirement, USAO-centered prosecutions) rest on a single outlet, and the Public Integrity Section staffing and 'chief election fraud prosecutor' reports appear only in a Senate Democrats' letter of 2026-06-08, which was not relied on. Not checked: Justice Manual Title 9 election provisions, unpublished Attorney General orders or delegations, and the 'Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses' handbook (reported removed from the DOJ website; not verified). The Lawfare account of the Eastern District of Missouri U.S. attorney's authority is secondhand. The match field is parallel because EO 14248 and the U.S. attorney directions are related election-enforcement actions. The California Globe article date is taken from the letter date (the page says the letters went out on a Tuesday).
